Facebook Dating Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Profiles and Protect Yourself

Scammers on Facebook dating profiles are skilled at building trust quickly — but warning signs can help you pause, verify, and avoid sending money.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-20 · 16 min read

Facebook dating scam UKfake Facebook dating profileromance scam Facebook
Quick answer: Facebook dating scammers build an emotional connection over weeks, then invent an emergency that needs your money — a money request is by itself enough reason to stop and treat the contact as high risk. If you have already sent money, call your bank straight away (159 connects you to its fraud team) and report the crime to Report Fraud.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What is a Facebook dating scam?

A Facebook dating scam happens when a criminal creates a fake profile — often using stolen photos — and targets you through Facebook Dating or direct messages. The scammer's goal is to build an emotional connection with you over weeks or months, then ask for money. The requests usually start small (a few pounds for a meal or transport) and escalate to larger sums for supposed emergencies, medical bills, business investments, or travel costs to meet you in person.

Some scammers also use the relationship to trick you into sharing personal information, which they then use for identity theft or to blackmail you. The scam is effective because it exploits loneliness and the ordinary human desire for connection — not because victims are careless. Victims often feel embarrassed to report it because they have developed genuine feelings for a person who turned out not to exist. The criminal may rely on that embarrassment to discourage reporting.

Warning signs of a fake Facebook dating profile

No single sign proves a profile is fake. Each one below shifts the odds, and several appearing together is a strong reason to stop and verify before you send money or share personal details.

  • Stolen or generic photos — the profile picture looks professionally taken or like a stock image, and a reverse image search shows the same photo used elsewhere online. Plenty of real people have flattering photos, so treat a match as a prompt to dig further rather than a verdict on its own.
  • Vague or inconsistent personal details — they claim a specific profession but give evasive answers about their work, location, or family, and the story shifts each time they tell it. Inconsistency over time matters more than any single vague answer.
  • Reluctance to video call — they make excuses (broken camera, poor internet, work restrictions) whenever you suggest a video call or meeting. Some genuine people are camera-shy or have real constraints, but a pattern of excuses stretching over weeks, especially alongside money requests, is a serious concern.
  • Fast emotional escalation — within days or weeks they say they love you, want to marry you, or talk about a shared future, far faster than the relationship would warrant.
  • Requests for money or financial information — cash for emergencies, travel, medical treatment, business opportunities, or debts. They may also ask for bank details, card numbers, or passwords. A money request is enough reason not to pay and to treat the interaction as high risk; you do not need another warning sign before stopping.
  • Isolation tactics — they discourage you from telling friends or family about the relationship, or suggest the people close to you are jealous and trying to break you up.
  • Requests to move off Facebook — they push early to move conversations to WhatsApp, Telegram, or email, away from Facebook's reporting and monitoring systems.
  • Messaging that does not fit the conversation — replies that read as copy-pasted, answer a question you did not ask, or arrive in a rhythm suggesting several people share the account. Judge the fit between question and answer, not the standard of the English itself. Many genuine people on UK dating platforms write in a second or third language, and treating imperfect English as evidence of fraud will cost you real connections while missing the fluent scammers entirely.

How the scam unfolds from first contact to money loss

The scam typically begins when the fake profile sends you a message or likes your photo. They will compliment you, ask personal questions, and seem genuinely interested. Over the following weeks they build rapport by messaging regularly, sharing false details about their life, and expressing affection. They may send small gifts to make the relationship feel real. Once they believe you are emotionally invested, they introduce a problem: a family emergency, a business deal needing funding, medical bills, or travel costs to visit you.

They ask if you can help — often starting with a small amount to test whether you will comply. If you send money, they thank you profusely and promise to repay you, then create another emergency and ask for more. Some victims have sent thousands of pounds over months.

Two variants are worth knowing. In the first, the scammer asks you to receive money into your bank account and pass it on, claiming they cannot access UK banking. They may be trying to use you as a money mule. Do not receive or forward money for them, and contact your bank immediately if any funds have already arrived. Accounts used to move criminal funds can be frozen or closed, and knowingly continuing after you suspect where the money came from can lead to a criminal investigation or prosecution.

In the second, there is no money request at all — the scammer patiently collects your full name, address, date of birth, and identity document details, which are then sold or used to open credit in your name.

How to verify if a Facebook dating profile is genuine

If you are unsure whether someone is real, work through these checks before sending money or sharing personal information. None is conclusive alone, but together they can help you make a more informed assessment.

Ask them to video call. Use Messenger's video call feature or suggest WhatsApp video. A video call does not prove identity or intentions, and some genuine people may be reluctant, but repeated excuses over time are a warning sign — especially when they appear just as the conversation turns to meeting or money.

Reverse-image search their profile photo. Go to Google Images, click the camera icon, and upload the photo. If it appears on modelling sites, stock libraries, or other dating profiles under different names, that is strong evidence the profile is not genuine, though it does not prove who created it or how the image was obtained. A clean result is weaker evidence than a match — it means the photo is not in the indexes, not that the person is real.

Search their name and stated details — workplace, hometown, university — and see whether a consistent real person emerges. Ask specific questions about their life and note whether answers stay consistent over weeks.

Look at the shape of the account. Long posting history, tagged photos from friends, and a friends list mixing family, colleagues, and school friends are all harder to fake than a profile photo. A sparse account is common among scammers, but also among people who simply do not use Facebook much or who set up a fresh profile after a breakup — weigh it alongside everything else rather than on its own.

Be cautious with cover stories that conveniently explain why someone can never meet or video call — deployed military officer, offshore oil rig worker, surgeon on an overseas contract. These are heavily used precisely because they pre-empt the obvious question.

And if they ask for money, stop and do not pay. The request alone is enough to treat the interaction as high risk, however close you feel and however plausible the emergency sounds.

What to do immediately if you have already sent money or shared details

Act quickly — speed materially affects whether the money comes back.

Contact your bank or payment provider straight away. Call the number on the back of your card, use your banking app, or call 159, which connects you to your bank's fraud team on a number scammers cannot spoof. Ask them to attempt a recall of the payment.

If you paid by bank transfer, you may be entitled to be reimbursed. Since 7 October 2024, UK payment firms have operated under mandatory reimbursement rules for authorised push payment (APP) fraud, which includes romance scams where you were deceived into authorising the payment yourself. The rules cover eligible Faster Payments and CHAPS transfers between UK accounts. Report the claim promptly and no later than 13 months after the final payment. Your bank should normally reimburse an eligible claim within five business days, up to a maximum of £85,000.

Your firm may apply an excess of up to £100, and some may choose to waive it; neither the excess nor the gross-negligence exception can be applied if the firm assesses you as a vulnerable consumer. Limited exclusions apply, so cooperate with reasonable questions from your bank. You do not need to prove the scammer's identity or catch them. If your bank refuses, make a formal complaint and ask for its final response in writing; you can then take the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is free.

Different payment methods take different routes. If you paid by debit or credit card, contact the card issuer immediately and ask whether it can attempt a chargeback under the card-scheme rules. Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act is not general scam reimbursement: it may apply only to a qualifying credit-card purchase costing more than £100 and no more than £30,000 where the supplier breached the contract or misrepresented what was being supplied. Money transfer services such as Western Union or MoneyGram should be contacted immediately to try to halt a transfer still in transit.

PayPal payments you sent deliberately should be reported through PayPal's scam reporting route, not as an unauthorised transaction — an unauthorised claim means someone used your account without permission, and reporting it that way will be investigated and rejected on the facts, costing you time.

Report the scam to Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) on 0300 123 2040 or at reportfraud.police.uk. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101 instead — Report Fraud does not cover Scotland. Ask for a crime reference number and keep it; your bank or a later dispute process may ask for it.

If you shared personal information such as your name, address, date of birth, or identity document details, apply for Cifas Protective Registration. This places a flag against your name in the National Fraud Database, so lenders carry out extra checks before opening credit in your name. It is a paid service and it will slow down your own credit applications — that is the point of it. Then check your credit file with the three UK credit reference agencies: Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion.

Each is required to provide statutory access to your file, and checking all three matters because lenders do not all report to the same agency.

Do not send any more money, whatever they say — including if they now claim they can release your earlier payments once you cover one final fee. That follow-up demand is a standard part of the script, not a change in the situation.

Reporting the scam in the UK

Report the fake profile to Facebook. In Facebook Dating, open Matches or your conversations, tap through to the profile or conversation, then use Options and choose Report. For a standard Facebook profile outside Dating, use the three-dot menu on the profile and select the reporting option, choosing the fake account or scam category. Facebook will investigate and may remove the profile, though this takes time and you should not wait on it before contacting your bank.

Report the crime to Report Fraud (formerly Action Fraud) on 0300 123 2040 or at reportfraud.police.uk, which handles fraud reports for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland and shares intelligence with police forces. In Scotland, report to Police Scotland on 101.

If you received suspicious emails or links, forward them to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If you received scam text messages, forward the text to 7726, free of charge. These routes are for suspicious messages only — they are not a route for reporting the romance scam itself, and they will not reach anyone who can act on a crime report.

Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 can help you understand your rights and next steps. Victim Support on 0808 168 9111 offers free, confidential emotional support, independently of the police, and you do not need to have reported the crime to use it.

Keep everything as evidence: messages, screenshots of the profile before it disappears, the profile URL, payment references, and bank correspondence. Scammers delete accounts quickly once they are challenged, and evidence you did not capture is usually gone for good. The more people who report the same profile, the faster Facebook and law enforcement can connect it to other victims.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get my money back if I sent it to a Facebook dating scammer?

Often, yes — more often than most people expect. For eligible Faster Payments or CHAPS transfers between UK accounts made on or after 7 October 2024, mandatory reimbursement rules mean your bank should normally reimburse an eligible APP fraud claim within five business days, up to £85,000. Report promptly and no later than 13 months after the final payment. A firm may apply an excess of up to £100, but it cannot apply the excess or the gross-negligence exception if it assesses you as a vulnerable consumer. Romance scams are covered: being deceived into authorising the payment yourself is precisely what these rules address, and you do not have to identify or catch the scammer to qualify. If you paid by card, ask the issuer whether it can attempt a chargeback; Section 75 applies only to qualifying credit-card purchases involving breach of contract or misrepresentation, not to scam payments generally. Money transfer services such as Western Union should be contacted immediately in case the transfer can still be stopped. PayPal payments you sent deliberately should be reported through PayPal's scam route rather than as an unauthorised transaction. Report to your bank first and fastest, then to Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. If your bank declines to reimburse you, make a formal complaint and ask for its final response in writing; you can then take the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is free to use.

What should I do if the scammer is threatening me or asking me to send explicit photos?

Do not send any images, and do not pay. Paying does not end it — it signals you will pay again. Preserve evidence before you block: screenshot the threats, the profile, and the profile URL. Once you block, you may lose access to the conversation, and the police and the platform will both want it. Then report the profile to Facebook using the reporting tools on the profile or conversation. If you are in immediate danger call 999. Otherwise call the police on 101 — in Scotland, 101 reaches Police Scotland directly. Threatening to share intimate images is a criminal offence in the UK, and the police can act on it. For specialist help, the Revenge Porn Helpline on 0345 6000 459 supports adults facing intimate image abuse and can work with platforms to get content removed. StopNCII.org lets you create a digital fingerprint of an image from your own device — the image itself is never uploaded — which participating platforms including Facebook use to block it from being shared. If you are under 18, contact Childline's Report Remove service instead. Victim Support on 0808 168 9111 provides free emotional support throughout. Do not report this to report@phishing.gov.uk. That inbox handles suspicious emails and nothing else — no one there can act on image abuse or a threat against you.

Is it safe to meet someone from a Facebook dating profile in person?

Meeting someone you have only known online carries risk, particularly if you have not video called them. Use a video call and reverse-image search as preliminary checks, while remembering that neither proves identity or intentions. If you do meet, tell a trusted friend or family member where you are going, who you are meeting, and when you expect to be back, and arrange to check in with them. Meet in a public place in daylight, never at their home or a private location, and arrange your own transport there and back so you are not dependent on them to leave. If they do not match their photos, or anything else feels wrong, leave — you owe a stranger no explanation. If they ask for money before or during the meeting, do not pay and treat the situation as high risk.

How can I tell if someone's Facebook profile is real before I start chatting?

Look at the whole account rather than any single feature. Genuine profiles often have a history of posts and photos, tagged photos posted by other people, a friends list mixing different parts of their life, and details that stay consistent across the profile. Reverse-image search the main photo — if it turns up on modelling sites or on other dating profiles under a different name, that is strong evidence the profile is not genuine, but not proof of who created it. A friends list made up almost entirely of attractive strangers with minimal activity is a common pattern on fake accounts. None of this is conclusive. Real people delete old posts, keep locked-down privacy settings, or start fresh profiles after a breakup, and a sparse account is not evidence of fraud on its own. Use these checks to decide how much caution to apply, not to convict someone. A video call can be a useful check, but it does not establish identity or prove the person's intentions. Any request for money is enough reason not to pay and to treat the interaction as high risk.

What if I have already fallen in love with someone and now I am worried they might be a scammer?

That worry is worth taking seriously, and having it does not make you foolish — these scams are run by organised criminals who are practised at this. Ask for a video call. It can provide useful evidence, but it cannot establish identity or intentions on its own. Refusal or a fresh excuse is a strong warning sign. Ask specific questions about their life and see whether the answers hold up over time, and search their name and details online. If they have asked for money at any point, do not pay and treat the interaction as high risk regardless of how convincing the reason was. Talk to a trusted friend or family member too — being emotionally involved makes patterns genuinely hard to see from the inside, which is why scammers work to isolate you from the people who would spot them. If you have already sent money, read the section above on reimbursement before you assume it is gone. Recovery may still be possible, and being deceived by a practised criminal is not your fault. For emotional support, Victim Support on 0808 168 9111 and Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 are both free and confidential.
